segs.text: Module one, objective one. What pharmacokinetics is, and the disciplines around it. A drug given as a dosage form, such as a tablet, follows one path: it dissolves, enters the systemic circulation and moves to and from the tissues, where it produces its effect, and it is metabolized and excreted. Pharmaceutics covers the first stretch, from the dosage form up to the drug in solution. Pharmacokinetics, P K, covers everything after that point. She said, We don't consider the drug being into the body until it is in solution and able to pass through some of those membranes. So P K describes the rates at which the drug moves into, through and out of the body.

card.m: dosage form → drug in solution → systemic circulation → tissues and back → effect
pharmaceutics: dosage form → drug in solution
pharmacokinetics (PK): drug in solution → circulation, tissues, metabolism, excretion → effect
PK: the rates of drug moving into and out of the body

segs.text: In short, P K is the study of A D M E: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. Absorption is the passage of drug molecules from the administration site into the systemic circulation. Distribution is the reversible transfer of a drug to and from the site of measurement; it is reversible because drug moves back out of the tissues as well as into them. Metabolism is the conversion of one chemical species to another, also called biotransformation. Excretion is the removal of intact drug or metabolite from the body. Other faculty add a letter, an L for liberation or a T for toxicology, but in this course it is these four.

card.m: PK = ADME
absorption: administration site → systemic circulation
distribution: reversible, to and from the site of measurement
metabolism: one chemical species → another (biotransformation)
excretion: removal of intact drug or metabolite
this course: ADME, four letters

segs.text: The quickest way to separate P K from pharmacodynamics, P D, is what each one relates. P K follows concentration against time: after a dose, how the drug level changes from hour to hour. P D is the relationship between drug concentration at the site of action and the pharmacological response, so it follows concentration against response. The textbook gives the direction: higher doses produce higher drug concentrations, more drug at the receptor site and a more intense effect, up to a maximum effect. So the effect rises as the concentration rises, but not in proportion to it, because the effect cannot rise above that maximum. She said, Pharmacokinetics, we're looking at concentration and time. Pharmacodynamics, we're looking at concentration and effect.

card.m: PK: concentration and time
PD: concentration at the site of action → response
higher dose → higher concentration → stronger effect, up to a maximum
effect rises with concentration, but not in proportion: it stops at the maximum

segs.text: Several neighbouring disciplines use P K for a particular purpose, such as treating patients, comparing groups or judging safety. The first is biopharmaceutics: how the drug's physicochemical properties, the dosage form and the route of administration together affect the rate and extent of systemic absorption. These three matter because the drug must first dissolve and then pass through membranes, so its balance between lipid and water solubility, the product it is in and the place it is given change how much is absorbed and how fast. Rate means how fast the drug is absorbed, and extent means how much of the dose is absorbed.

card.m: biopharmaceutics: properties + dosage form + route → rate and extent of absorption
dissolve, then cross membranes: lipid and water solubility matter
rate: how fast   extent: how much

segs.text: The other disciplines related to P K each have a one line definition. Clinical pharmacokinetics is applying pharmacokinetic methods to drug therapy. Population pharmacokinetics is the study of pharmacokinetic differences between population groups, such as older adults, children, pregnant women, immunocompromised patients and patients with a disease. Clinical toxicology is the study of adverse effects of drugs and toxic substances in the body. Toxicokinetics is applying pharmacokinetic principles to drug safety evaluation studies.

card.m: clinical PK: PK methods applied to drug therapy
population PK: differences between groups, e.g. geriatric, pediatric, pregnant, disease
clinical toxicology: adverse effects
toxicokinetics: PK in drug safety studies

segs.text: Her questions read out a definition almost word for word, and the options are bare discipline names, so you go from definition to name. In her poll the stem gave the biopharmaceutics definition, and the options were biopharmaceutics, toxicology, pharmacodynamics and pharmacology. The answer was biopharmaceutics, though a few students chose pharmacodynamics. P D is about response, not absorption, and pharmacology is not one of the disciplines this module defines. The key words decide it: absorption from dosage form and route means biopharmaceutics, response means P D, drug therapy means clinical P K, population groups means population P K, and safety studies means toxicokinetics. The E in A D M E is excretion; elimination, which also counts metabolism, is a separate term in objective three.

card.m: stem: properties, dosage form, route → rate and extent of absorption
biopharmaceutics ✓
✗ PD: response, not absorption   ✗ pharmacology: not defined here
absorption → biopharm   response → PD   drug therapy → clinical PK   groups → population PK   safety → toxicokinetics
E in ADME = excretion, not elimination
